# Sustainable Tourism Development Plan
## For a region with natural and heritage assets, entering the international market

**The central insight:** in tourism development, the binding constraint is almost never *demand*. It is **absorptive capacity** — how many visitors a place can take before the thing they came for degrades, and before the residents who host them turn against the industry. Demand can be switched on in eighteen months with a media buy and three airline route subsidies. Capacity takes a decade to build and can be destroyed in three seasons. Most regional tourism strategies fail because they are demand strategies wearing sustainability language.

So this plan inverts the usual order. **Capacity, distribution and local ownership are built first; international marketing is the last lever pulled, and it is pulled selectively.** Everything below follows from that.

**Illustrative case used throughout:** a sub-national region — call it the Region — with a UNESCO-tentative-list historic town (pop. 12,000), a national park with an alpine lake, ~40 villages, a small international airport 90 minutes away, current volume ~800,000 annual visitors of whom ~15% are international, and average international stay of 1.8 nights. Figures are illustrative; the structure transfers.

---

## 0. Four decisions to make before any marketing brief exists

**1. Choose your volume/value position explicitly — it is a governance decision, not a marketing preference.**
There are three viable models and they are mutually exclusive in practice:

| Model | Economics | Environmental load | Failure mode |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Volume** — high arrivals, low spend, day-trippers and cruise/coach | Revenue in transport and large operators; little sticks locally | Highest per-euro-retained | Overtourism, resident revolt, asset degradation |
| **Value** — fewer arrivals, longer stays, higher local spend | Revenue in accommodation, food, guiding, craft | Lowest per-euro-retained | Exclusion of residents from their own region; elite-capture optics |
| **Hybrid, zoned** — value in fragile zones, managed volume in built-up hubs | Mixed; requires active management | Manageable if zoning is enforced | Zoning collapses under commercial pressure |

For a region whose core assets are a small historic town and a national park, **the hybrid-zoned model is the only defensible answer** — but it must be written into planning law, not a strategy PDF. If you cannot enforce zoning, you have chosen the volume model whether you say so or not.

**2. Your seasonal and geographic concentration is a bigger problem than your total volume.**
800,000 visitors is not a load problem. 800,000 visitors of whom 60% arrive in ten weeks and 70% visit two sites *is* a load problem. **The primary planning target is dispersion — across the calendar and across the map — not growth.** This single reframe changes what you build, what you market, and what you count.

**3. Decide now who captures the value, because infrastructure decides it and infrastructure is irreversible.**
A 300-room international-brand resort on the lake shore and forty upgraded family guesthouses generate similar bed-nights and radically different local retention (roughly 20–30% vs. 65–80% of visitor spend staying in-region, depending on procurement). Whichever you permit in the first five years sets the industrial structure for thirty. **Zoning, licensing and credit access are your real economic-benefit policy.** Community-benefit funds are a rounding error by comparison.

**4. You are the cause of your own overtourism.**
No agency decides to ruin a place. It happens because the agency's KPI is arrivals, its budget is justified by arrivals, and the minister announces arrivals. Every mechanism below is defeated by an arrivals-only scorecard. **Change the metric first (§6), or accept that the rest of this is decoration.**

---

## 1. Unbundle: "sustainable tourism" is six distinct problems with six distinct instruments

Conflating these is the most common and most expensive error in the field. Each column has its own failure signature and its own correct tool; applying the wrong tool wastes money and builds false confidence.

| | **Physical carrying capacity** | **Cultural integrity** | **Local economic retention** | **Resident consent** | **Carbon & transport** | **Governance & institutional capacity** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Content** | Trail erosion, lake water quality, waste and sewage load, parking, peak-hour crowding at 2–3 chokepoints | Sacred/ritual sites, living traditions vs. staged performance, resident privacy, language, festival authenticity | Leakage to external operators, OTA commissions (15–25%), imported food and materials, seasonal precarious labour | Housing displacement to short-term rentals, price inflation, loss of everyday amenity, "we can't use our own square" | Long-haul flights = 60–80% of trip footprint; car dependency in-region | Fragmented mandates (park agency, heritage body, municipalities, DMO), no data, no enforcement teeth |
| **Failure signature** | Degraded asset, emergency closures, negative reviews citing crowds | Museumification; young people leave; traditions performed for money and abandoned in private life | Growth with no local income gain → political backlash against tourism itself | Anti-tourism protest, hostile hosting, regulatory whiplash | Reputational exposure; certification failure; stranded strategy | Beautiful strategy, zero implementation |
| **Wrong instrument** | "Awareness campaigns" and visitor codes of conduct | Folklore festival funding | A community benefit fund | Consultation meetings after decisions are made | Carbon offsets purchased centrally | Another strategy document |
| **Right instrument** | Timed entry, quotas, pricing, physical redesign of chokepoints, dispersion of demand | Community-controlled access protocols; consent-based interpretation; guide licensing | Procurement rules, licensing structure, credit access, direct-booking infrastructure | Statutory veto/consent thresholds and revenue that residents can see and control | Length-of-stay strategy + in-region public transport, not offsets | One accountable authority with pooled budget and enforcement power |

**The critical connection:** five of these six columns are solved primarily by the *same* two moves — **dispersion (across season and space) and local ownership of supply.** That is a fortunate structural fact and it should organise the whole programme. Longer stays in more places, hosted by locally-owned businesses, simultaneously reduce chokepoint load, raise retention, lower per-visitor carbon (amortising the flight), and preserve resident amenity. The sixth column — governance — is the precondition for all of it.

---

## 2. The diagnostic to run before spending anything: capacity and leakage

Two numbers, both knowable in one season, that most agencies never calculate.

### 2a. Chokepoint capacity audit

For each of the top 8–10 sites, establish: **physical capacity** (safety and flow limit), **ecological capacity** (the level above which measurable degradation occurs — trail widening, water quality, wildlife behaviour change), **experiential capacity** (the level at which visitor satisfaction declines — measurable by survey), and **social capacity** (the level at which resident tolerance declines).

The binding limit is the lowest of the four, and it is **almost always experiential or social, not physical.** This matters enormously: it means "the site can hold 2,000 people" is the wrong answer to the wrong question. A historic town square can physically hold 2,000 and is ruined for everyone at 600.

| Site | Current peak day | Binding capacity (type) | Gap | Instrument |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Historic town core | 6,200 | ~2,800 (social — resident amenity) | **−3,400** | Timed entry, coach cap and relocation of coach parking, off-peak pricing |
| Lake main shore | 4,100 | ~1,800 (ecological — water quality, shoreline) | **−2,300** | Hard quota, permit system, shuttle-only access |
| Summit trail | 900 | ~700 (experiential) | −200 | Booking system, staggered start times |
| Monastery / sacred site | 1,400 | Community-determined | To be set by custodians | **Consent protocol, not a number the agency sets** |
| Secondary villages (×12) | 40–120 | 400–800 (physical/experiential) | **+3,000 headroom** | Product development and routing — this is where growth goes |
| Winter/shoulder season, all sites | — | Large headroom | **+ substantial** | Seasonal product; the cheapest capacity you own |

**Read the last two rows again.** The region does not need fewer visitors; it needs the *same or more* visitors distributed into ~3,000 person-days of daily village headroom and eight months of unused calendar. Dispersion is not a compromise between growth and sustainability — it is the only route to both.

### 2b. Leakage audit — where does €100 of visitor spend go?

Trace a representative international trip through the value chain. Illustrative baseline for the Region:

| Spend line | Share of trip budget | Retained in-region | Retained € |
|---|---|---|---|
| International flight | 35% | ~0% | 0 |
| Accommodation (mix of external-brand hotel and local guesthouse) | 25% | ~45% | 11 |
| Food and beverage | 15% | ~55% (imported inputs, external supply chains) | 8 |
| Tours, guiding, entry | 10% | ~50% (external tour operators, OTA commission) | 5 |
| Retail and craft | 8% | ~35% (imported souvenirs) | 3 |
| In-region transport | 7% | ~70% | 5 |
| **Total (ex-flight)** | **65%** | — | **≈32 of 65** |

**Retention on in-region spend: ~49%.** The three biggest recoverable losses, in order:

1. **Imported food inputs** — a farm-to-guesthouse sourcing programme is the single highest-leverage economic intervention available and requires no visitor behaviour change.
2. **OTA commission and external tour operators** — a regional direct-booking platform and licensed local guiding requirement.
3. **Imported souvenirs** — a certified regional origin mark with enforcement.

Closing these to ~65% retention is worth more to local income than a 30% increase in arrivals — **with zero additional environmental load.** This is the calculation that justifies the entire plan to a finance ministry, and it should be on the first slide.

---

## 3. Price the status quo: what unmanaged growth actually costs

The case for restraint must be made in cash, not values, because the case for volume always is.

| | |
|---|---|
| Baseline: 800k visitors, 15% international, €12m annual local tourism income (retained) | — |
| **Path A — unmanaged growth to 1.6m over 6 years** | |
| Gross visitor spend growth | +100% |
| Retained local income (retention falls to ~35% as external operators scale) | +43% |
| Peak-season chokepoint load | +140% → **emergency closures likely by year 4** |
| Waste/water/sewage capex forced, unbudgeted, on emergency timelines | **€18–30m, 40–60% cost premium vs. planned** |
| Housing: short-term-rental conversion in historic core | 8% → 30% of stock; **local rents +45%** |
| Resident support for tourism (survey) | 72% → **below 40%; the political precondition collapses** |
| Reputational trajectory | "Must-see" → "ruined, go before/instead" within one guidebook cycle |
| Recovery cost after a degradation event (asset closure + repositioning) | **8–15 years; often never for a mid-tier destination** |
| **Path B — managed dispersion, 1.15m over 6 years** | |
| Gross visitor spend growth | +52% |
| Retained local income (retention rises to 65%) | **+82% — higher absolute local income than Path A** |
| Peak load at chokepoints | **−10%** |
| Programme cost (governance, capacity systems, product development, capability building) | **~€22m over 6 years, planned** |

**One slide, one sentence:** managed dispersion delivers *more local income than unmanaged doubling*, at lower environmental load, lower capital cost, and without spending the region's political and reputational capital. The volume path is not merely riskier — on the metric that matters (retained local income), **it is worse on its own terms.**

---

## 4. The intervention ladder — climb it in order

Order matters more than content. Marketing before capacity is the canonical failure.

| Tier | Content | Cost | Time | Reversibility |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0 — See it** | Chokepoint capacity audit (all four capacity types); leakage audit; resident sentiment baseline with village-level breakdown; cultural asset inventory built **with** custodian communities, including a "not for tourism" list; existing-visitor segmentation (who already comes, what they spend, why they leave after 1.8 nights) | Low (€0.4–0.8m) | 6–9 months | Total |
| **0b — Govern it** | Single accountable destination authority with pooled budget and enforcement power; resident and custodian representation with **defined consent thresholds, not advisory seats**; visitor data system; short-term-rental registration and cap in the historic core **legislated before demand grows** | Low–moderate | 9–15 months | Moderate |
| **1 — Contract for it** | Guide licensing tied to cultural and environmental training; accommodation licensing conditional on local sourcing and employment standards; origin certification mark for craft and food; tour operator accreditation with claim-scope rules on cultural content; procurement rules for publicly-funded tourism assets | Low | 6–12 months | High |
| **2 — Build capacity and product** | Chokepoint physical redesign and relocation of coach/car parking; timed-entry and quota systems; shuttle network and rail/bus integration; **village cluster product development (the growth engine)**; shoulder and winter season product; guesthouse upgrade credit line; farm-to-guesthouse supply programme; direct-booking platform | Moderate–high (€14–18m) | 18–36 months | Moderate |
| **3 — Market it, selectively** | Segment-targeted international acquisition into *pre-built* dispersed capacity (§5); route development aligned to length-of-stay goals; trade and media programmes | Moderate | 24 months+ | High |
| **4 — Restructure** | UNESCO inscription (with a management plan that can survive it — inscription is a demand shock and must be treated as one); protected-area status extension; regional rail investment; cross-border itineraries | High | 5–15 years | Low |

**Design rules.**
- **Tier 0 and 0b are unconditional.** Without one accountable authority, everything below is uncoordinated.
- **Never market a site you have not yet given the capacity to receive visitors.** Marketing is the fastest, cheapest and most irreversible lever; it is therefore last.
- **Legislate short-term-rental controls before demand arrives**, not after. Retrofitting them means expropriating value from residents who have already invested — politically near-impossible. This is the single most time-sensitive item in the plan.
- **UNESCO inscription is not a reward; it is a load event.** Do not pursue it until Tier 2 is complete.

---

## 5. The international marketing strategy — demand shaping, not demand generation

The brief is not "attract more international visitors." It is **attract the visitors whose behaviour the region can absorb profitably** — and this is a targeting and product problem far more than a communications problem.

### 5a. Segment on behaviour, not demographics or interests

The relevant axes are **length of stay, seasonal flexibility, dispersion willingness, and local-spend propensity.**

| Segment | Stay | Season | Disperses? | Local spend | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Slow-travel cultural independents** (35–65, high education, 2–4 week trips) | 5–8 nights | Flexible | **Yes** | High | **Primary** |
| **Active/outdoor multi-day** (hiking, cycling, water) | 4–7 nights | Shoulder-favouring | **Yes, by design** | Medium–high | **Primary** |
| **Regional short-break neighbours** (short-haul, repeat) | 2–3 nights | **Off-peak capable** | Yes with product | Medium | **Primary — best carbon profile per night** |
| **Special interest** (gastronomy, craft, ornithology, pilgrimage) | 4–6 nights | **Season-defined, often off-peak** | Yes | High | **Primary** |
| Mainstream long-haul touring (fixed itinerary, coach) | 1–2 nights | Peak | No | Low | Manage, do not court |
| Cruise/day-trip excursion | 0 nights | Peak | No | **Lowest** | **Cap, price, or decline** |
| Peak-season leisure volume | 3–5 nights | Peak only | No | Medium | Neutral; do not stimulate |

**The strategic move:** stop selling the region and start selling **routes and seasons.** Marketing a place produces concentration at its most famous point. Marketing a *seven-night route through four village clusters in October* produces exactly the behaviour the capacity audit says you need. Product structure does the dispersion work that messaging cannot.

### 5b. Sequence: earn credibility before buying reach

1. **Trade and specialist intermediaries first.** For slow-travel and special-interest segments, specialist operators and guidebooks convert far more efficiently than consumer advertising, and they can be *contractually* bound to itinerary, group-size and local-supplier rules. Distribution is a policy instrument — use it.
2. **Earned and editorial second**, built on genuinely differentiated substance: the sourcing programme, the community-owned guiding, the seasonal traditions that exist independently of tourism.
3. **Owned channels and direct booking third.** Every direct booking is 15–25% of spend recovered.
4. **Paid consumer media last, and narrowly** — geo-targeted at short-haul off-peak segments and retargeted at declared-interest audiences. Never paid brand advertising for peak season at chokepoint sites. You are buying a problem.

### 5c. Message discipline: the rule the previous case earned

**Do not market what you cannot deliver, and do not market what you have decided to protect.**

- No imagery of restricted, sacred or "not for tourism" sites — *ever*, including in stock libraries and influencer briefs. A photograph is a promise; a photograph of a place you will not let people visit is a promise you will break at the gate.
- No empty-landscape imagery of chokepoints at peak. It sets an expectation the site cannot meet, and crowd disappointment is the most common driver of negative reviews.
- **Cultural content requires custodian consent, and consent is specific, revocable and written.** Communities decide what is interpreted, how, and by whom. The tourism agency does not own the region's culture and should say so publicly.
- Communicate the rules as part of the appeal, not as friction: quotas, timed entry and permits are *quality guarantees*. Destinations that explain scarcity honestly attract the segments that value it. **Restraint is the positioning.**

---

## 6. Change the scorecard, or nothing above survives

The plan's fate is decided here. Arrivals must be demoted from headline metric to input variable.

| Retire | Adopt | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Total arrivals | **Retained local income per visitor** (from the leakage audit, re-run annually) | The actual objective |
| Bed-nights (gross) | **Average length of stay**, and **bed-nights outside the top-2 zones** | Directly measures dispersion |
| Peak-season occupancy | **Off-peak occupancy** and **seasonality ratio (peak month ÷ lowest month)** | The cheapest capacity you own |
| — | **Resident support for tourism, by village, annually, published** | The binding political constraint; a leading indicator of everything |
| — | **Chokepoint days above capacity threshold** | The environmental and experiential constraint |
| — | **Local ownership share of licensed accommodation and guiding** | Determines who benefits, and thus consent |
| — | **Local sourcing share of food and craft spend** | Highest-leverage retention lever |
| — | **Short-term-rental share of historic-core housing stock** | Displacement early-warning |
| — | **Carbon per visitor-night** (declining with length of stay) | Credibility and long-run market access |

**Institutionalise it or lose it.** Publish the dashboard annually and unedited. Tie the destination authority's budget and executive incentives to the dispersion and retention metrics — not to arrivals. Give the resident and custodian bodies a statutory trigger: if resident support in any village falls below a defined threshold, marketing spend directed at that village is suspended pending review. **A metric a community can pull a lever with is a governance mechanism; a metric in a report is a press release.**

---

## 7. Where this plan fails, honestly

Any plan that cannot state its own failure modes is marketing.

1. **Political time-preference.** Ministers need arrivals numbers before the next election; this plan's returns land in years 4–8. *Mitigation:* front-load the leakage-recovery programme — sourcing, direct booking, guide licensing raise local income within 12–18 months with no volume growth. That is your early political win, and it is real.
2. **Enforcement capacity.** Zoning, rental caps and licensing are worthless unenforced. *Mitigation:* budget enforcement headcount explicitly as a line item at Tier 1, and prefer instruments that are self-enforcing by design (quota booking systems, licensing gates) over those requiring inspection.
3. **Elite capture of the "value" model.** High-value positioning can price residents out of their own region and hand the upside to a few well-capitalised operators. *Mitigation:* resident access rights and free/discounted local entry to all managed sites; guesthouse credit lines and cooperative structures at Tier 2; ownership-concentration caps in licensing.
4. **Long-haul carbon.** Attracting long-haul visitors is in structural tension with any credible climate commitment. Offsets do not resolve this. *Mitigation:* be honest about it — prioritise short-haul and rail-accessible markets, and treat length-of-stay as the primary genuine lever (a 7-night trip has half the per-night flight footprint of a 3.5-night trip). State the trade-off publicly rather than greenwashing it.
5. **Success is the risk.** A viral moment, a film location, or UNESCO inscription can deliver a demand shock that outruns capacity in a single season. *Mitigation:* build the quota and timed-entry infrastructure *before* you need it, and pre-agree the surge protocol — including the authority to suspend marketing and cap access — with the destination authority board.
6. **Cultural commodification is gradual and hard to see.** No single decision causes it. *Mitigation:* the annual custodian review with revocable consent, and a standing rule that communities may withdraw any element from the tourism offer without justification or penalty.

---

## First 90 days

| Week | Action |
|---|---|
| 1–2 | Commission chokepoint capacity audit and leakage audit; appoint interim destination authority lead |
| 3–6 | Resident sentiment baseline by village; begin custodian consultation on cultural asset inventory and the "not for tourism" list |
| 4–8 | **Draft short-term-rental registration and historic-core cap legislation** — the most time-sensitive item in the plan |
| 6–10 | Existing-visitor segmentation from current data; identify the 12 village clusters with capacity headroom |
| 8–12 | Design the scorecard (§6) and secure ministerial agreement to retire arrivals as the headline metric — **in writing, before any marketing budget is approved** |
| 10–12 | Launch farm-to-guesthouse sourcing pilot in 2 clusters (early, visible, local-income win) |
| 12 | Board decision on volume/value/hybrid model, formally recorded, with zoning map attached |

**The one-line summary for the minister:

| Retail and craft | 8% | ~35% (imported souvenirs) | 3 |
| In-region transport | 7% | ~70% | 5 |
| **Total (ex-flight)** | **65%** | — | **≈32 of 65** |

**Retention on in-region spend: ~49%.** The three biggest recoverable losses, in order:

1. **Imported food inputs** — a farm-to-guesthouse sourcing programme is the single highest-leverage economic intervention available and requires no visitor behaviour change.
2. **OTA commission and external tour operators** — a regional direct-booking platform and licensed local guiding requirement.
3. **Imported souvenirs** — a certified regional origin mark with enforcement.

Closing these to ~65% retention is worth more to local income than a 30% increase in arrivals — **with zero additional environmental load.** This is the calculation that justifies the entire plan to a finance ministry, and it should be on the first slide.

---

## 3. Price the status quo: what unmanaged growth actually costs

The case for restraint must be made in cash, not values, because the case for volume always is.

| | |
|---|---|
| Baseline: 800k visitors, 15% international, €12m annual local tourism income (retained) | — |
| **Path A — unmanaged growth to 1.6m over 6 years** | |
| Gross visitor spend growth | +100% |
| Retained local income (retention falls to ~35% as external operators scale) | +43% |
| Peak-season chokepoint load | +140% → **emergency closures likely by year 4** |
| Waste/water/sewage capex forced, unbudgeted, on emergency timelines | **€18–30m, 40–60% cost premium vs. planned** |
| Housing: short-term-rental conversion in historic core | 8% → 30% of stock; **local rents +45%** |
| Resident support for tourism (survey) | 72% → **below 40%; the political precondition collapses** |
| Reputational trajectory | "Must-see" → "ruined, go before/instead" within one guidebook cycle |
| Recovery cost after a degradation event (asset closure + repositioning) | **8–15 years; often never for a mid-tier destination** |
| **Path B — managed dispersion, 1.15m over 6 years** | |
| Gross visitor spend growth | +52% |
| Retained local income (retention rises to 65%) | **+82% — higher absolute local income than Path A** |
| Peak load at chokepoints | **−10%** |
| Programme cost (governance, capacity systems, product development, capability building) | **~€22m over 6 years, planned** |

**One slide, one sentence:** managed dispersion delivers *more local income than unmanaged doubling*, at lower environmental load, lower capital cost, and without spending the region's political and reputational capital. The volume path is not merely riskier — on the metric that matters (retained local income), **it is worse on its own terms.**

---

## 4. The intervention ladder — climb it in order

Order matters more than content. Marketing before capacity is the canonical failure.

| Tier | Content | Cost | Time | Reversibility |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0 — See it** | Chokepoint capacity audit (all four capacity types); leakage audit; resident sentiment baseline with village-level breakdown; cultural asset inventory built **with** custodian communities, including a "not for tourism" list; existing-visitor segmentation (who already comes, what they spend, why they leave after 1.8 nights) | Low (€0.4–0.8m) | 6–9 months | Total |
| **0b — Govern it** | Single accountable destination authority with pooled budget and enforcement power; resident and custodian representation with **defined consent thresholds, not advisory seats**; visitor data system; short-term-rental registration and cap in the historic core **legislated before demand grows** | Low–moderate | 9–15 months | Moderate |
| **1 — Contract for it** | Guide licensing tied to cultural and environmental training; accommodation licensing conditional on local sourcing and employment standards; origin certification mark for craft and food; tour operator accreditation with claim-scope rules on cultural content; procurement rules for publicly-funded tourism assets | Low | 6–12 months | High |
| **2 — Build capacity and product** | Chokepoint physical redesign and relocation of coach/car parking; timed-entry and quota systems; shuttle network and rail/bus integration; **village cluster product development (the growth engine)**; shoulder and winter season product; guesthouse upgrade credit line; farm-to-guesthouse supply programme; direct-booking platform | Moderate–high (€14–18m) | 18–36 months | Moderate |
| **3 — Market it, selectively** | Segment-targeted international acquisition into *pre-built* dispersed capacity (§5); route development aligned to length-of-stay goals; trade and media programmes | Moderate | 24 months+ | High |
| **4 — Restructure** | UNESCO inscription (with a management plan that can survive it — inscription is a demand shock and must be treated as one); protected-area status extension; regional rail investment; cross-border itineraries | High | 5–15 years | Low |

**Design rules.**
- **Tier 0 and 0b are unconditional.** Without one accountable authority, everything below is uncoordinated.
- **Never market a site you have not yet given the capacity to receive visitors.** Marketing is the fastest, cheapest and most irreversible lever; it is therefore last.
- **Legislate short-term-rental controls before demand arrives**, not after. Retrofitting them means expropriating value from residents who have already invested — politically near-impossible. This is the single most time-sensitive item in the plan.
- **UNESCO inscription is not a reward; it is a load event.** Do not pursue it until Tier 2 is complete.

---

## 5. The international marketing strategy — demand shaping, not demand generation

The brief is not "attract more international visitors." It is **attract the visitors whose behaviour the region can absorb profitably** — and this is a targeting and product problem far more than a communications problem.

### 5a. Segment on behaviour, not demographics or interests

The relevant axes are **length of stay, seasonal flexibility, dispersion willingness, and local-spend propensity.**

| Segment | Stay | Season | Disperses? | Local spend | Priority |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Slow-travel cultural independents** (35–65, high education, 2–4 week trips) | 5–8 nights | Flexible | **Yes** | High | **Primary** |
| **Active/outdoor multi-day** (hiking, cycling, water) | 4–7 nights | Shoulder-favouring | **Yes, by design** | Medium–high | **Primary** |
| **Regional short-break neighbours** (short-haul, repeat) | 2–3 nights | **Off-peak capable** | Yes with product | Medium | **Primary — best carbon profile per night** |
| **Special interest** (gastronomy, craft, ornithology, pilgrimage) | 4–6 nights | **Season-defined, often off-peak** | Yes | High | **Primary** |
| Mainstream long-haul touring (fixed itinerary, coach) | 1–2 nights | Peak | No | Low | Manage, do not court |
| Cruise/day-trip excursion | 0 nights | Peak | No | **Lowest** | **Cap, price, or decline** |
| Peak-season leisure volume | 3–5 nights | Peak only | No | Medium | Neutral; do not stimulate |

**The strategic move:** stop selling the region and start selling **routes and seasons.** Marketing a place produces concentration at its most famous point. Marketing a *seven-night route through four village clusters in October* produces exactly the behaviour the capacity audit says you need. Product structure does the dispersion work that messaging cannot.

### 5b. Sequence: earn credibility before buying reach

1. **Trade and specialist intermediaries first.** For slow-travel and special-interest segments, specialist operators and guidebooks convert far more efficiently than consumer advertising, and they can be *contractually* bound to itinerary, group-size and local-supplier rules. Distribution is a policy instrument — use it.
2. **Earned and editorial second**, built on genuinely differentiated substance: the sourcing programme, the community-owned guiding, the seasonal traditions that exist independently of tourism.
3. **Owned channels and direct booking third.** Every direct booking is 15–25% of spend recovered.
4. **Paid consumer media last, and narrowly** — geo-targeted at short-haul off-peak segments and retargeted at declared-interest audiences. Never paid brand advertising for peak season at chokepoint sites. You are buying a problem.

### 5c. Message discipline: the rule the previous case earned

**Do not market what you cannot deliver, and do not market what you have decided to protect.**

- No imagery of restricted, sacred or "not for tourism" sites — *ever*, including in stock libraries and influencer briefs. A photograph is a promise; a photograph of a place you will not let people visit is a promise you will break at the gate.
- No empty-landscape imagery of chokepoints at peak. It sets an expectation the site cannot meet, and crowd disappointment is the most common driver of negative reviews.
- **Cultural content requires custodian consent, and consent is specific, revocable and written.** Communities decide what is interpreted, how, and by whom. The tourism agency does not own the region's culture and should say so publicly.
- Communicate the rules as part of the appeal, not as friction: quotas, timed entry and permits are *quality guarantees*. Destinations that explain scarcity honestly attract the segments that value it. **Restraint is the positioning.**

---

## 6. Change the scorecard, or nothing above survives

The plan's fate is decided here. Arrivals must be demoted from headline metric to input variable.

| Retire | Adopt | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Total arrivals | **Retained local income per visitor** (from the leakage audit, re-run annually) | The actual objective |
| Bed-nights (gross) | **Average length of stay**, and **bed-nights outside the top-2 zones** | Directly measures dispersion |
| Peak-season occupancy | **Off-peak occupancy** and **seasonality ratio (peak month ÷ lowest month)** | The cheapest capacity you own |
| — | **Resident support for tourism, by village, annually, published** | The binding political constraint; a leading indicator of everything |
| — | **Chokepoint days above capacity threshold** | The environmental and experiential constraint |
| — | **Local ownership share of licensed accommodation and guiding** | Determines who benefits, and thus consent |
| — | **Local sourcing share of food and craft spend** | Highest-leverage retention lever |
| — | **Short-term-rental share of historic-core housing stock** | Displacement early-warning |
| — | **Carbon per visitor-night** (declining with length of stay) | Credibility and long-run market access |

**Institutionalise it or lose it.** Publish the dashboard annually and unedited. Tie the destination authority's budget and executive incentives to the dispersion and retention metrics — not to arrivals. Give the resident and custodian bodies a statutory trigger: if resident support in any village falls below a defined threshold, marketing spend directed at that village is suspended pending review. **A metric a community can pull a lever with is a governance mechanism; a metric in a report is a press release.**

---

## 7. Where this plan fails, honestly

Any plan that cannot state its own failure modes is marketing.

1. **Political time-preference.** Ministers need arrivals numbers before the next election; this plan's returns land in years 4–8. *Mitigation:* front-load the leakage-recovery programme — sourcing, direct booking, guide licensing raise local income within 12–18 months with no volume growth. That is your early political win, and it is real.
2. **Enforcement capacity.** Zoning, rental caps and licensing are worthless unenforced. *Mitigation:* budget enforcement headcount explicitly as a line item at Tier 1, and prefer instruments that are self-enforcing by design (quota booking systems, licensing gates) over those requiring inspection.
3. **Elite capture of the "value" model.** High-value positioning can price residents out of their own region and hand the upside to a few well-capitalised operators. *Mitigation:* resident access rights and free/discounted local entry to all managed sites; guesthouse credit lines and cooperative structures at Tier 2; ownership-concentration caps in licensing.
4. **Long-haul carbon.** Attracting long-haul visitors is in structural tension with any credible climate commitment. Offsets do not resolve this. *Mitigation:* be honest about it — prioritise short-haul and rail-accessible markets, and treat length-of-stay as the primary genuine lever (a 7-night trip has half the per-night flight footprint of a 3.5-night trip). State the trade-off publicly rather than greenwashing it.
5. **Success is the risk.** A viral moment, a film location, or UNESCO inscription can deliver a demand shock that outruns capacity in a single season. *Mitigation:* build the quota and timed-entry infrastructure *before* you need it, and pre-agree the surge protocol — including the authority to suspend marketing and cap access — with the destination authority board.
6. **Cultural commodification is gradual and hard to see.** No single decision causes it. *Mitigation:* the annual custodian review with revocable consent, and a standing rule that communities may withdraw any element from the tourism offer without justification or penalty.
